Read a Parquet file

Source: R/aaa_parquet.R
morie_read_parquet.Rd

Native Parquet reader: no nanoparquet, no arrow. Handles the v1 format with PLAIN, RLE and dictionary encodings, GZIP (one or more gzip members a page), Snappy, Zstandard (ZSTD) or no compression. ZSTD pages are read by a decoder in the package (RFC 8878, without dictionaries), so no other package is needed for them; the writer does not write ZSTD. Nested and repeated columns are refused.

Usage

morie_read_parquet(path, columns = NULL)

Arguments

path

Path to a .parquet file (opened once, only when it is a regular file, and read a page at a time, never held whole), or the file's bytes as a raw vector.

columns

Optional character vector of column names to decode; the rest are skipped entirely. character(0) gives a data frame with the file's rows and no columns. A name the file gives two columns names the first of them.

Value

A data.frame. Every error the reader raises, a missing or damaged file included, starts with parquet:; no base-R warning escapes it (a value a damaged file makes R warn about is an error instead).

Details

A string column comes back as text marked UTF-8 (ASCII text stays unmarked, as R keeps it). A Parquet string is UTF-8 by definition, and morie_write_parquet() refuses to write anything else, so a value that is not valid UTF-8, or that holds a NUL byte, is refused with a parquet: error naming the column: returned, it would fail later in nchar() or toupper().

Three options bound what a file can make the reader do, each checked from the file's footer and page headers before anything is allocated or inflated: rmoriedata.parquet_max_rows (default 5e7 rows), rmoriedata.parquet_max_page_bytes (default 2^30 bytes a page) and rmoriedata.parquet_max_text_bytes (default 2^32 bytes, 4 GiB). The last is the most text and fixed-length bytes the compressed pages of one file may inflate to, summed over the columns read; pages stored uncompressed are not counted. A file past a bound is refused with an error naming the option to raise.

A DECIMAL is a double: its scaled value, exact when the unscaled whole number is below 2^53 and the scale at most 22, otherwise the nearest double to the whole number, divided by the power of ten, with a warning that it is rounded. One whose whole number is past the range of a double, or whose precision and scale the format does not allow for its type, is refused. A UUID is text ("8-4-4-4-12" lower-case hexadecimal), and a FLOAT16 a double. Other fixed-length bytes (an INTERVAL, or bytes with no logical type) are refused by name.

An INT32 column is an integer column unless one of its values cannot be an R integer, which is -2147483648 (-2^31, R's NA_integer_): then the whole column is a double. This is decided once for the whole column, across all its pages and row groups, from the values in its rows: an entry of a dictionary that no row uses does not count. Columns of 8 and 16 bits (stored as INT32) are integer columns, and an unsigned 32-bit column is a double column, whether the file marks the type by its converted type (UINT_8, INT_16, UINT_32, ...) or by its logical type (INT(8, false), as arrow writes uint8, ...). A value outside the marked width (an unsigned 8-bit column holding 256, or the word 0xFFFFFFFF, which is -1 as an INT32) is a damaged file and is refused, naming the column and the value, as other values the format does not allow are; so is a width the format does not give the stored type (an INT32 marked 64 bits wide, an INT64 marked 8, 16 or 32). Every 32- and 64-bit word is a value of its width, signed or unsigned. Every other 64-bit column is a double column: exact below 2^53, otherwise the nearest double, with a warning that it is rounded.

Where a column's logical type and its converted type disagree (UINT_32 with a signed INT(32), or with an unsigned INT(8)), the logical type is read, as the format says and arrow does, for every type: the converted type is read only when the file gives no logical type.

A TIMESTAMP (in milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds, or the legacy INT96) is a POSIXct in UTC, and a TIME a difftime in seconds. Each is the double nearest to its exact number of seconds, rounded once and without a warning. A POSIXct is a double: it holds about 16 significant digits, so within 2^33 seconds (272 years) of 1970 it resolves a microsecond and around 2025 steps of about 238 nanoseconds; a time in nanoseconds is the nearest such value, not the nanosecond itself.

Column names are the file's names exactly: an empty name stays "", a name used twice stays twice, and no name is changed to make it syntactic or unique (text that is valid UTF-8 is marked UTF-8). A file with no columns reads as a data frame of its rows and no columns.
